analysis.one_liner: Gives the FDA authority to regulate cigarettes and smokeless tobacco, including advertising, flavors, and product standards.
analysis.headline: Despite 123 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill never got a House vote; it sat in a Health subcommittee until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make cigarettes and other tobacco products the first products of their kind regulated by the FDA, the agency that already polices food and drugs. Tobacco makers would have to register annually, disclose their ingredients, submit to factory inspections, and get government approval before selling new or 'reduced risk' products. The bill would ban candy-like flavorings added to cigarettes, allow tougher warning labels, and let the Secretary restrict advertising that reaches teenagers, while leaving tobacco farming untouched and reserving to Congress any decision to ban a product outright.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who the bill's findings describe as the main targets of tobacco advertising; current smokers, who would get accurate ingredient disclosure and honest health claims; and taxpayers, whose health care costs the bill's own findings put at $75 billion in potential savings from cutting youth smoking in half.

how_it_helps.text: The bill classifies tobacco products as items the FDA can regulate, subjecting manufacturers to annual registration, ingredient disclosure, records inspection, and user fees for the first time.

It bans cigarettes from containing characterizing flavorings other than tobacco or menthol, including strawberry, clove, cinnamon, and cocoa, which health advocates argued were used to ease first-time smokers into the habit.

It requires premarket approval of all new tobacco products and gives the Secretary power to require prior approval of health claims for 'reduced risk' products, so makers of 'light' and 'low tar' cigarettes could no longer market them as safer without proof.

The bill's findings state that tobacco causes over 400,000 deaths a year and that cutting youth smoking by half would prevent more than 10 million of today's children from becoming regular smokers, saving over 3 million from premature death.

It gives the Secretary authority to restrict the sale, distribution, advertising, and promotion of tobacco products where needed to protect public health, and to require public notification or recall of unreasonably harmful products.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear compliance costs, advertising and promotion restrictions, premarket approval requirements, and user fees. Tobacco retailers and the marketing and advertising businesses that serve tobacco makers lose promotional revenue. Tobacco growers are untouched: the bill expressly excludes the growing and curing of raw tobacco from FDA authority.

drawbacks.text: The flavor ban expressly excludes menthol, the one flavor with the largest share of Black adult smokers, leaving menthol cigarettes on the market untouched.

The bill caps regulation in several ways: it forbids any minimum purchase age above 18, forbids restricting sales to pharmacies or prescription-style controls, and reserves to Congress alone any decision to ban a product or cut nicotine to zero.
It exempts tobacco farming entirely from FDA authority, so the raw-leaf supply chain stays unregulated, and it is silent on tobacco taxes and on funding smoking-cessation programs.

Compliance costs fall on manufacturers and would likely be passed into retail prices, and defenders of the industry argued at the time that the agency's new user fees and paperwork would burden small makers more than the largest companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health payoff is large by the bill's own numbers: tobacco is the leading preventable cause of death, and most new users start as minors. The real costs are regulatory burden and higher prices for smokers, and the bill has genuine design compromises: menthol is carved out, the purchase age is frozen at 18, the raw-leaf supply is exempt, and Congress keeps a veto over the two most aggressive steps a regulator could take. Even with those compromises, the public-health upside outweighs the compliance burden, which is why the eventual version of this proposal drew support from both public-health groups and at least one major tobacco company.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which passed it along to its Health subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the two-year Congress expired.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Davis introduced the bill on March 17, 2005, with 28 original cosponsors from both parties, including Henry Waxman and other longtime advocates of FDA tobacco regulation.
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on March 22 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.

No subcommittee or committee vote, no House floor action, and no Senate companion action ever followed; the bill accumulated 123 cosponsors, 91 Democrats and 32 Republicans, but died at the end of the 109th Congress on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they kept selling cigarettes with no FDA ingredient disclosure, no premarket review of new or 'reduced risk' products, and no federal restrictions on advertising and flavorings for another several years. Tobacco retailers and growers also kept the status quo, since the bill never advanced far enough to impose even its own carve-outs and limits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco makers, unregulated another four years

for.name: Rep. Tom Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family Smoking Prevention and Tobacco Control Act on March 17, 2005.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor; he was the leading House advocate for giving the FDA authority over tobacco.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for health legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Health on March 22, 2005, and never reported it or scheduled a markup during the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Presided over the committee that took no action on the bill during the 109th Congress.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal FDA regulation of tobacco, the issue this bill was written to settle; the largest company's support for the FDA-approval approach came only alongside provisions like the menthol carve-out that smaller rivals rejected.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan: 123 cosponsors split 91 Democrats and 32 Republicans, with a Republican lead sponsor. The bill stalled inside a committee controlled by the Republican majority rather than dying on a partisan floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would subject cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers to FDA registration, ingredient disclosure, inspections, premarket approval of new products, and advertising restrictions, ending their decades-long status as the only consumer product of their kind sold without federal health regulation. Its profits depend on recruiting new smokers, so its interest runs against the bill's youth-prevention goals.

industries.industry: Tobacco retailers (convenience stores and other outlets)
industries.note: The bill bars any rule that would prohibit face-to-face tobacco sales by a category of retail outlet or set a purchase age above 18, so it keeps cigarettes on ordinary store shelves permanently even as it regulates how they are made and marketed.

The bill expressly exempts the growing, cultivation, and curing of raw tobacco from FDA authority and bars FDA employees from entering tobacco farms without written consent, keeping the raw-leaf supply chain outside regulation.

industries.industry: Advertising and marketing agencies serving tobacco
industries.note: The tobacco industry spent over $12.4 billion on marketing in 2002 under the bill's findings, much of it aimed at reaching young people; the bill allows restrictions on advertising and promotion, cutting a revenue stream for the agencies that provide it.
